text:
Recent work supports perturbing interaction histories to measure recommendation dependence. Oh and Cho’s [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) introduces a recency-bias metric and reports that excessive recency emphasis harms performance across their evaluated models. Scarcelli et al.’s [Demystifying Sequential Recommendations (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) searches for minimal history changes that alter recommendations using genetic algorithms, evaluating targeted and untargeted counterfactuals across three datasets and three models. A [2026 temporal-attribution study](https://jidmis.org/index.php/jidmis/article/view/2525) evaluates deletion faithfulness, counterfactual stability, sufficiency, and masking-versus-shuffling consistency; its findings show architecture-dependent reliance on recent versus broader history.

Suggested diagnostic synthesis: on unchanged training-history prefixes, remove equal numbers of recent interactions, interactions representing repeated interests, and isolated interactions; compare each intervention against multiple length-matched random deletions. Define repeated interests using recurring item IDs where available or explicit title/description similarity, without assuming unavailable categories. Measure original top-item rank displacement, score-margin changes, and top-10 overlap using identical candidate sets and eligibility masks. Compare deletion with position-preserving masking and order shuffling to distinguish content dependence from sequence-length and positional effects. Stratify by history length and recurrence. These are proposed controls, rather than an established protocol from the cited papers: deletion sensitivity demonstrates model dependence, but cannot alone establish causal user preference or temporal shortcut learning. Use macro validation HR@10 to assess whether changes motivated by these probes improve the benchmark.
